Gridding And Bernstein Degree

Documents/Bernstein Polynomial/Gridding And Bernstein Degree

The Two Independent Choices

Section titled “The Two Independent Choices”

Every coefficient-backed object has two related but different discretizations:

  • the physical parameter grid partitions the scheduling domain into cells;
  • the scalar Bernstein Degree chooses how many local coefficient matrices represent the polynomial in every cell.

Throughout the manual, ρs(j)\rho_s^{(j)}ρs(j)​ denotes node jjj on axis sss, so Gs={ρs(1),…,ρs(ks)}\mathcal G_s=\{\rho_s^{(1)},\ldots,\rho_s^{(k_s)}\}Gs​={ρs(1)​,…,ρs(ks​)​}. The full grid is

G=G1×⋯×Gℓ,Nnode=∏s=1ℓks,Ncell=∏s=1ℓ(ks−1).\mathcal G=\mathcal G_1\times\cdots\times\mathcal G_\ell, \qquad N_{\mathrm{node}}=\prod_{s=1}^{\ell}k_s, \qquad N_{\mathrm{cell}}=\prod_{s=1}^{\ell}(k_s-1).G=G1​×⋯×Gℓ​,Nnode​=s=1∏ℓ​ks​,Ncell​=s=1∏ℓ​(ks​−1).

A physical hypercube is indexed by the one-based vector c=(c1,…,cℓ)\mathbf c=(c_1,\ldots,c_\ell)c=(c1​,…,cℓ​). Its local Bernstein coefficients use zero-based tensor labels: C(c)[i]C^{(\mathbf c)}[\mathbf i]C(c)[i]. Only the one-dimensional case shortens c\mathbf cc to the scalar ccc.

Adding a grid node makes more physical cells. Raising Degree makes more Bernstein labels inside each existing cell. Neither action is a shorthand for the other. Degree 1 is the simplest affine case, not the package target: finite nonnegative degrees represent continuous piecewise-polynomial data on the same physical partition.

One-Dimensional Input

Section titled “One-Dimensional Input”

For one scheduling parameter, pdmat and pdvar accept a numeric vector as shorthand for a one-element cell array. The vector must be finite, strictly increasing, and have at least two entries.

Here rhoGrid has three nodes, so it creates two physical intervals. Degree 2 gives the three local labels 0, 1, and 2, hence three coefficients per interval. The global input has five entries because its required length is

(k1−1)m+1=(3−1)2+1=5.(k_1-1)m+1=(3-1)2+1=5.(k1​−1)m+1=(3−1)2+1=5.

The shared value 12 is the common boundary coefficient of the two global degree-two cells. It is a Bernstein coefficient, not an extra physical grid node and not necessarily a sampled function value. Adjacent pdvar cells share this complete face value, but their cell-local derivatives need not match. This is value continuity, not a B-spline or a global differentiability claim.

Two-Dimensional Input

Section titled “Two-Dimensional Input”

For two scheduling parameters, pass one node vector per axis. A global coefficient source is a MATLAB cell array whose dimensions follow the two axes:

There are 3×2=63\times2=63×2=6 physical rectangles. The axes deliberately use different node counts. The common degree is 1 along both axes, so each rectangle has (1+1)2=4(1+1)^2=4(1+1)2=4 local tensor coefficients. Their flat package order is the row order returned by A.lbls():

The same order explains A.coeffs([1 1]). The first grid dimension varies more slowly in that local-label order. Physical cells, in contrast, are stored as a nested tree: LocalValues{c1}{c2}. Thus A.LocalValues{2}{1} selects the second cell along the first axis and the first cell along the second.

For this degree-one example, the global coefficient-grid dimensions are

(k1−1)m+1=(4−1)1+1=4,(k2−1)m+1=(3−1)1+1=3,(k_1-1)m+1=(4-1)1+1=4, \qquad (k_2-1)m+1=(3-1)1+1=3,(k1​−1)m+1=(4−1)1+1=4,(k2​−1)m+1=(3−1)1+1=3,

which is why data is a 4-by-3 cell array. For a global coefficient-backed pdmat, every axis must satisfy this shape rule.

The ell-Dimensional Case

Section titled “The ell-Dimensional Case”

The same convention extends directly to ℓ\ellℓ scheduling parameters:

If axis sss has ksk_sks​ nodes and the common scalar degree is m, the package has

Ncell=∏s=1ℓ(ks−1),Ncoeff/cell=(m+1)ℓ.N_{\mathrm{cell}}=\prod_{s=1}^{\ell}(k_s-1), \qquad N_{\mathrm{coeff/cell}}=(m+1)^\ell.Ncell​=s=1∏ℓ​(ks​−1),Ncoeff/cell​=(m+1)ℓ.

The physical-cell tree is LocalValues{c1}{c2}...{c_ell}. Its leaf is a flat cell array whose label rows come from lbls(); labels range independently from 0 through m in each coordinate. A global coefficient-backed pdmat uses one source-array dimension per parameter, of length (k_s - 1) * m + 1 on axis sss.

Degree is a single scalar property in the implemented package, not a per-axis degree vector. pdmat accepts any nonnegative integer degree; constructor-created pdvar accepts every finite nonnegative integer degree. Products may create higher-degree expressions through coefficient algebra.

Do Not Conflate These Operations

Section titled “Do Not Conflate These Operations”
Effects of grid, representation-degree, and decision-degree changes
OperationChanges physical cells?Changes coefficients per cell?Current package boundary
Add grid nodesYesNo, for a fixed degreeCommon-grid algebra is supported; there is no general public adaptive-subdivision command.
Raise or align Bernstein degreeNoYesExact degree elevation aligns compatible coefficient-backed operands.
Choose a higher pdvar decision degreeNoYesConstructor-created pdvar accepts every finite nonnegative integer degree.

The Bernstein Polynomial chapter gives the basis, local coordinate, degree-elevation formula, and coefficient-product rule. The pdmat constructor reference lists the accepted source forms, and the pdvar constructor lists its decision-variable forms.
